items.title: Theravada and Mahayana are the two major Buddhist traditions
items.claim: How do Theravada and Mahayana differ?

options.text: Theravada ('teaching of the elders') dominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos — emphasises the Pali Canon and arhat ideal; Mahayana ('great vehicle') dominant in East Asia and Vietnam — emphasises bodhisattva path and Sanskrit/Chinese sutras; Tibetan Vajrayana is sometimes treated as a third stream

items.reveal:
The split developed in the centuries after the Buddha's death, with the Second Council (around 100 years after his parinirvana) marking early disagreements. Mahayana texts (Prajnaparamita Sutras, Lotus Sutra) emerged from around the 1st century BCE.

The bodhisattva ideal — postponing one's own final liberation to help all beings — is central to Mahayana. Theravada acknowledges bodhisattvas (including the historical Buddha before his enlightenment) but emphasises the arhat ideal.

Tibetan Buddhism is often treated as a separate Vajrayana branch. Zen and Pure Land are East Asian Mahayana developments.
items.why: Calling Buddhism 'one religion' obscures real diversity. The traditions share core teachings but differ on the path, the goal, the authoritative texts, and the role of devotion.

items.title: Ashura commemorates Husayn's martyrdom at Karbala
items.claim: What is the significance of Ashura in Shia Islam?

options.text: A celebration of victory in battle
Commemoration of the martyrdom of Husayn ibn Ali (grandson of Muhammad) at Karbala on 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680 CE) — a defining event of Shia identity, marked with mourning rituals

items.reveal:
Husayn, his family and 72 followers refused allegiance to the Umayyad caliph Yazid I and were besieged then killed at Karbala (in modern Iraq). The event is recounted in detail in Shia narrative tradition (maqtal literature).

Muharram processions (matam) in Shia communities involve mourning, recitation, sometimes ritualised self-flagellation (different observances by region; many Shia clerics prefer blood donation as a modern alternative).

In Sunni Islam, 10 Muharram is also significant — Muhammad observed the day as a fast, having found Jewish residents of Medina fasting in commemoration of Moses's deliverance. Sunni observance is much quieter than Shia.
items.why: Religious calendars carry historical memory. Ashura, like Pesach, ritualises a specific historical wound — and the difference in how Sunnis and Shias mark the same date reveals the structural differences between the branches.

items.title: Samsara, karma and moksha are linked in Hindu cosmology
items.claim: How do samsara, karma and moksha relate?

options.text: Samsara is the cycle of birth, death and rebirth; karma is the moral causation that drives it; moksha is liberation from the cycle — typically by realising the unity of atman and Brahman
Karma punishes the wicked in this life only
Moksha is automatic at death for all souls

items.reveal:
Karma (action) produces fruits (phala) that bind the soul to future rebirths. Bad karma leads to lower rebirths (animal, hell realms); good karma to better ones (human, deva). All rebirth is conditioned and impermanent.

Moksha is the exit from samsara — variously achieved through jnana (knowledge), bhakti (devotion), karma (right action), or yoga (meditation). The Bhagavad Gita presents all four as legitimate paths.

Buddhism shares samsara, karma and liberation concepts but rejects atman — so 'rebirth' in Buddhism is the continuation of a causal stream, not a soul transmigrating.
items.why: Indian-origin religions share a family of concepts that differ in detail but contrast structurally with Abrahamic religions. The cyclic worldview shapes everything from ethics to attitudes towards death.
